extracted.intended_audience: postgraduate research students (Masters/PhD/MD) preparing a scientific-style thesis (NUI Galway audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for planning, drafting, formatting and submitting a scientific-style postgraduate thesis (Masters, PhD, MD), including organisation of chapters, supervisor interactions, and presentation/formatting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin writing early / keep a writing record
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is part of your research from the start; do not leave thesis writing to the end. Writing helps you to refine and reflect on ideas and record progress at different research stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate writing into your study from the outset so that the final write-up is less daunting. Use writing as a tool to keep track of development across research stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write regularly (make writing a habit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not wait until you feel 'ready' — writing is a skill developed by regular practice and should be integrated into your weekly routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat writing as an essential part of study rather than a separate, final task. Frequent short practice sessions improve skill: 'practice makes perfect.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in brief bursts (use timed sessions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break big writing tasks into smaller chunks and tackle them in short, timed writing sessions to maintain concentration and motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set time deadlines for each session. Short focused bursts are less intimidating and more productive than long, unfocused marathons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve distinct time for drafting (separate drafting from editing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not spend your dedicated writing time revising, editing, reading or formatting; writing time should be used to put new words on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on producing new text quickly without trying to be perfectly accurate. Get initial ideas down, then revise and edit them later; in scientific writing, reference as you write but leave detailed editing to separate sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcome writer's block (strategies and mindset)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writer's block is normal; treat writing as a series of drafts. Use methods such as relaxation, planning, mind maps, or working from figures/tables to free ideas and restart writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested tactics: relax; jot down unordered thoughts and then order them; create diagrams/mind maps of key points and expand; work on tables/figures first and structure text around them; write briskly knowing you will revise later. If blocked, discuss with supervisor and bring notes of techniques tried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act on feedback and revise promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Redraft in light of colleagues' and supervisors' feedback while suggestions are still fresh; thesis writing is a multi-stage process of reflection, revision and rewriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a first draft to have something tangible to work on. Print drafts to view from a different perspective; perform close edits (spelling, grammar, typography); check for overused words; ensure paragraph coherence and cohesion; consider adding more scholarly/empirical support where needed; take breaks and act on supervisor feedback promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a positive approach to writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach the writing process with vigour and enthusiasm, learn from mistakes and keep moving forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember that prior undergraduate writing experience is a foundation; frequent writing will make the process easier and build confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish ground rules with your supervisor (prepare and schedule meetings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supervisors guide research stages but are busy; prepare for meetings, arrange a regular series of meetings (e.g. weekly), and establish key points early for the write-up period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear outline or plan of action to your supervisor and submit only your best draft for review. Be clear about what support you need and ask specific, precise questions. Attempt to find answers yourself before asking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad issues to discuss with supervisor at start of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Key items to establish with your supervisor before beginning to write: timetable for completion, theoretical/conceptual framework, potential sources/further reading, research questions and design, statement of research contribution, methodology, analytical techniques, draft set of contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the checklist (Table 5.1) to structure initial discussions and ensure mutual understanding of expectations and milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matters of style to discuss with supervisor
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss style/formatting preferences with your supervisor, including typography (font style, size, spacing for drafts), which style guide to follow, formatting of headings/subheadings, and presentation of illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agree on conventions at the start to ensure consistency and to comply with School/College/University requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow University Guidelines for Research Degree Programmes
rubrics_metrics.description: Check and follow the University's formal guidelines for formatting, required sections (Abstract, Acknowledgements, Appendices, Declarations, supplementary material), and submission procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is the student's responsibility to know and abide by prescribed rules; supervisors can assist with interpretation but do not absolve the student of responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include main sections of a scientific-style thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical monograph-format thesis contains: Introduction (including Literature Review), Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion, Bibliography/References. The order may vary by discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this outline as a general guideline; supervisors may advise adaptations. Each main section has specific purposes and expectations (see individual section criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction (including Literature Review) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide background, set up the main hypothesis and rational argument motivating experiments, make the purpose of the thesis clear, state specific objectives, and include a Literature Review that underpins the experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover all relevant literature that led to the experimental hypothesis and ensure material in the Literature Review has a clear purpose in developing arguments used later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials and Methods: completeness and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide full details of materials and procedures so another scientist could repeat the experiments; include material identification (genus, species, strain) and special characteristics (sex, age, genetic status) as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group related methods together, avoid putting results in this section, use precise accurate words/terms, list sources for materials, and consider writing this section early as it is straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results: present core data clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Results are the core contribution, usually presented in one or more chapters in the past tense; state results clearly and simply as your contribution to knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each chapter may follow the research article format (Introduction, Materials & Methods, Results, Discussion). Provide specific methods for that chapter's experiments and place non-essential data in Appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion: analyse and integrate findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Return to the main hypothesis and discuss whether results support or reject it; compare and integrate results across experiments; highlight principal results leading to conclusions and explain their significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely recapitulate results; identify exceptions or lack of correlation openly; comment on practical applications and theoretical implications; summarise major findings and provide evidence for each conclusion and a statement of acceptance/rejection of the unifying thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography / References: correct citation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a full account of all literature used and cited; check with supervisor for the correct citation/reference system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reference management programs (e.g., EndNote) and their 'cite while you write' features to keep track of references and maintain an up-to-date bibliography; refer to library guides as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article-based format thesis requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An article-based thesis comprises a number of research articles united by a comprehensive introductory chapter and an explanation of how each article relates to the overall research question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student contributions to multi-author papers must be explicit; concluding chapter should state how objectives were met and critically evaluate article results; supplementary appendices may be needed to provide methodological detail for reproducibility; follow College-specific minimum published-article requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title page: required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The title page must include: full title and subtitle; total number of volumes and volume number if multiple; full name of author (with qualifications/distinctions if desired); the qualification for which the thesis is submitted; name of the institution; college/school/discipline; month and year of submission; name of Head of School/Discipline; names of supervisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow University Guidelines for exact formatting and required details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis title quality (accurate, concise, avoid waste words and jargon)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good title is the fewest possible words that adequately describe the content; it should be accurate and concise, avoid 'waste words' (e.g., 'A', 'An', 'The', 'Investigations into', 'Studies on', 'Observations on'), refrain from abbreviations/jargon, and use specific terms (e.g., genus/species/strain when appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose word order carefully (avoid ambiguous placement of words like 'using'); ensure titles aid indexing and retrieval in databases; avoid overly general or overly long titles with redundant words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of Contents: placement and level of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The Table of Contents should immediately follow the title page and not be overly detailed; it lists headings/sub-headings with corresponding page numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the lowest level of heading to display (avoid levels lower than sub-subheadings); use a consistent decimal numbering system (e.g., 1.0, 1.1, 2.2.1), consistent indentations, capitalization conventions (main headings full caps, other levels sentence case), and ensure page numbering conventions (preliminaries in lowercase Roman numerals). Provide separate Lists of Figures and Tables rather than listing them in the TOC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration regarding the work (originality statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The thesis must include a declaration certifying that the work is the student's own and that no degree has been obtained on the basis of the same work elsewhere; if based on group work, state the student's contribution explicitly with reference to collaborators' theses/publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the declaration accurately reflects individual contribution and any overlap with other works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An Abstract (no more than 300 words) summarises the thesis and is normally a single paragraph that clarifies objectives/scope, describes methods, summarises results, and outlines key conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use past tense; do not include tables, graphs, or references; do not include information not present in the thesis; ensure accuracy and precision; think of it as a condensed version of the whole thesis to help readers decide relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgements: what to include
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgements must (1) acknowledge technical assistance received (laboratory help, discussion, sources of special materials) and (2) refer to any external funding or financial assistance (fellowships, grants, contracts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be courteous and precise in wording; give appropriate credit to those who helped in the research.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of Abbreviations / Glossary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Three basic rules: use only standard abbreviations; do not use abbreviations in the Abstract or Title; do not use full stops with abbreviations except 'no.' When first using an abbreviation, spell out the full term followed by the abbreviation in parentheses; include such abbreviations in a Glossary placed after the Table of Contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep abbreviations to a minimum; in scientific theses include an SI statement above the List of Abbreviations indicating use of standard units/notations; when writing units, abbreviate when numerical values are given but not when numerals are not used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices: purpose and organisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendices contain material relevant to the main body but not suitable for inclusion there (e.g., detailed tables, large groups of illustrations, technical notes on methodology, data collection forms, copies of documents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place all Appendices at the end, separate different categories into separate Appendices with clear titles and number/letter them (Appendix 1 or Appendix A). Page numbers in Appendices should be separate (A-1, A-2, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Headings and subheadings formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Main chapter/section headings should be in bold type and full capitalization; subheadings and sub-subheadings should not be bold and should use sentence case (first word capitalized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For figure/table headings use capitalization of the first word only (e.g., 'Figure 1 Incidence of hospital-acquired infections'). Place table number and title above a table and figure number and title below a figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font size and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to University Guidelines for exact rules; generally use a readable font such as Times New Roman, 12 pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm specific font/style requirements with School/College/University guidelines before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Present work in either 1.5 or double spacing as a general rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the preferred spacing with your supervisor or University Guidelines for drafts vs final submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrations (figures and tables) — purpose and self-containedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Each figure or table must have a clear purpose and be self-contained so readers can understand it without reading surrounding text; give each figure/table a number and an informative title and ensure clear chapter-specific numbering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to each figure/table in the text before it appears; avoid abbreviations in figures/tables or provide a key; use software to make illustrations professional; number figures chapter-specifically (e.g., 1.1, 1.2) and number tables independently but similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures/graphs technical conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Label axes accurately and fully with units; plot the independent variable on the X axis and the dependent variable on the Y axis; avoid overcrowded graphs; ensure each line is easily distinguishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a figure is necessary (e.g., if there is one curve, text may suffice). Choose appropriate graph types to show trends vs exact values and avoid cramming too much information into a single graph.
